episodes.title: Ep1: Viktor Popovic — An immigrant founder who rebuilt after losing Google traffic overnight now routes merchant payments in real time to expose the hidden fees his first company’s margins never revealed.
episodes.hook: An immigrant founder who rebuilt after losing Google traffic overnight now routes merchant payments in real time to expose the hidden fees his first company’s margins never revealed.
episodes.summary:
Viktor Popovic rebuilt after 21 years running Ultimate Washer by creating Avendo, a platform that routes each merchant transaction in real time across multiple processors so the lowest price wins without any lock-in. The most striking detail is that he now charges processors only ten cents per successful transaction and nothing to merchants, a direct response to the opaque statements and stagnant rates he accepted for over a decade.

- After 14 years with one processor, Viktor saw volume grow while rates stayed fixed because statements were four to ten pages of line items that owners handed to accountants rather than challenge.
- Avendo collects one application and set of documents, then forwards them to multiple processors; once several underwrite the merchant, the system lets those processors bid live on every card transaction.
- The merchant dashboard shows only the final approved amount, statement, and chargeback tools; all routing logic, fallback decisions, and price responses stay hidden in the backend and complete in milliseconds.
- A queue was added after live testing showed that transaction logging, not authorization, created stalls; the two backend teams met, mapped the bottleneck, and inserted the queue so results could be written without blocking the flow.
- Weekly rotating tests now run across system segments to catch similar issues before they scale, because the architecture must duplicate cleanly for future markets such as Canada.
- Viktor’s prior experience with seven separate product databases taught him that disconnected tools force constant manual updates; Avendo’s teams therefore meet at least weekly to keep every new component on a single source of truth.

Viktor Popovic is Founder and President of Avendo.

episodes.title: Ep2: Dr. Michael Brandt — Inside a dual-certified facial plastic surgeon's practice where skin-cancer reconstruction and elective facelifts share the same anatomy and demand identical standards for natural function.
episodes.hook: Inside a dual-certified facial plastic surgeon's practice where skin-cancer reconstruction and elective facelifts share the same anatomy and demand identical standards for natural function.
episodes.summary:
In his Nerra Voices interview, Dr. Michael Brandt states that skin-cancer reconstruction and elective facelifts demand identical precision in tissue handling, planning, and scar camouflage because both must meet the same functional and aesthetic standard. He describes this shared requirement through the “supermarket test,” where a successful result lets the patient pass unnoticed so that others see the person rather than the work. The discussion also covers how his MSc research on scars changed his daily evaluation of outcomes and why he treats fillers and surgery as distinct tools rather than substitutes.

- Dr. Brandt notes that reconstruction after cancer removal often requires creative tissue movement to preserve surrounding structures, while aesthetic cases allow more control over incision placement, yet both receive the same attention to detail.
- His MSc work on scar assessment showed that the overall gestalt—how a scar sits relative to facial contours and affects expression—drives patient perception more than isolated factors such as color or texture.
- He applies the supermarket test to decide when a repair has failed: any distortion of eyelid position or unnatural tension means the result draws attention instead of blending in.
- Fillers can camouflage a nasal bump or restore volume but cannot reposition descended tissues or remove excess skin, so he does not use repeated injections as a bridge when structural correction is needed.
- Training and dual certification required years of delayed personal time; he now prioritizes evenings and family activities after health issues reminded him where his primary responsibility lies.
- Every case, whether reconstructive or cosmetic, creates an ongoing relationship because the surgeon continues to worry about long-term results rather than completing a one-time intervention.

Dr. Michael Brandt is a dual-certified facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon at FORM Face + Body in Toronto.

episodes.title: Ep3: Scott Pulcini — A scalper who once handled a tenth of E-mini volume rebuilt a durable edge by…
episodes.hook: A scalper who once handled a tenth of E-mini volume rebuilt a durable edge by reading iceberg orders and stop runs after algorithms erased his original speed advantage, then teaches the resulting rule set to retail traders.
episodes.summary:
Scott Pulcini once lost $800,000 in minutes on two separate days after breaching his own $100,000 daily loss limit instead of stopping. He rebuilt a durable edge after algorithms erased his original speed advantage by shifting from visible counterparties to reading stop runs and iceberg orders through CME MBO data on Bookmap, then codified the resulting rules into courses for retail traders.

- Scott once averaged 50,000 contracts a day—roughly 10 percent of E-mini S&P volume—by placing orders throughout the book and scalping around them while seeing every counterparty.
- After house numbers vanished, he adopted 2016 CME MBO data that reveals iceberg orders with certainty and treats them as the next-best proxy for where large entities are accumulating.
- He only acts on a stop or iceberg event inside zones that meet market-specific volume thresholds (700 contracts for S&P icebergs, 150 for crude or gold) drawn from nine years of observation.
- Entry waits for price to clear 115 percent of the five-minute ATR outside the zone; the stop sits on the far side so any breach must first clear trapped traders and the full volume event.
- The “dumb and dumber” setup flags retail stop runs that appear as strong initiative buying on candles but are usually liquidation that reverses once the ATR filter fails to confirm follow-through.
- A “sexy GEXie” adds conviction when a stop run lands at a heavy gamma level where options dealers must hedge, while reversion trades scalp back to the same volume event.
- Scott’s grandfather’s line “lose your head, lose your ass” became literal when two rule breaches cost him $800,000 apiece instead of the planned $100,000 daily stop.

Scott Pulcini is a former high-volume futures scalper who now teaches retail traders his stop-iceberg methodology and related strategies.

episodes.title: Ep4: Stuart Berkowitz — Translating scattered trial data into a public Bayesian atlas that models…
episodes.hook: Translating scattered trial data into a public Bayesian atlas that models upper-bound life-year gains from overlapping interventions while exposing every assumption for inspection.
episodes.summary:
Stuart Berkowitz says his public Bayesian models deliver an extra life year for 3.5 cents—far below any charity he has examined—by combining scattered trial data into joint probabilities that remove overlapping effects across interventions. He built 93 separate causal oracles that treat aging itself as a disease state and project optimized personal protocols reaching 111–135 years. The entire atlas is published so every assumption, extrapolation, and cross-correlation adjustment remains open to inspection.

- He started with VO2-max data from 122,000 Cleveland Clinic patients showing a 92 % all-cause mortality reduction at six standard deviations above the mean, then layered additional factors while subtracting cross-correlations.
- From 25 interventions the combinatorial space reaches 32 million possible bundles; front-door, back-door, and eigenvalue analyses on mechanism-of-action graphs are used to avoid double-counting benefits.
- Eigenvalue analysis removes most confounding, after which a measured 30–70 % residual correlation cut is applied and published inside each oracle.
- The site grew 51 % month-over-month with under $500 spent and no marketing, driven by visitors proxy-entering data for chronically ill friends or relatives.
- NHANES records are run through the oracles to quantify the gap between actual and optimal care; that gap is converted to life years via Social Security mortality tables and discounted by observed 50 % prescription adherence.
- Supplements show almost no role in disease-progression reduction for most conditions, though osteoarthritis, BPH, and preeclampsia register small measurable effects.
- A typical GP’s 300 chronic patients give doctors roughly 300-fold leverage over individual visitors when they adopt the Pareto-optimal lists.

Stuart Berkowitz builds and maintains the public Bayesian oracles at longevityresearch.ca that model maximal life-year gains across 93 diseases.

episodes.title: Ep5: Jason Shumard — A chiropractor who watched conventional care fail his mother
episodes.hook: A chiropractor who watched conventional care fail his mother now runs a virtual functional-medicine practice that treats Type 2 diabetes reversal as the measurable outcome and scales it with coaching teams.
episodes.summary:
Jason Shumard described testing 99 percent of diagnosed type 2 diabetics and finding toxin loads—mold, heavy metals, or environmental chemicals—while noting far lower rates in non-diabetics whose detoxification systems still function. His virtual functional-medicine practice therefore treats diabetes as cellular disease rather than a blood-sugar problem, scaling reversal through lab-guided protocols and coaching teams instead of direct physician visits. The measurable goal is healthier cells that naturally lower sugars, with patients required to remain under their own prescribing physicians.

- Stepped back from seeing patients himself to build and oversee a full team handling visits, marketing, and acquisitions so the mission could reach a million lives through ripple effects rather than solo work.
- Prioritizes toxin removal before liver or gut repair because toxins cause systemic damage; uses the triage analogy of stopping bleeding before treating a virus.
- Screens every new patient with symptom-tailored panels—comprehensive blood work, hormones, urine, stool, and full toxin testing—and refuses cases without an existing medical doctor supervising medications.
- States that 70 percent of healing comes from belief and motivation while only 30 percent comes from clinical steps, and therefore turns away prospects who want to be convinced rather than demonstrate strong internal drive.
- Tracks progress with the triglyceride-to-HDL ratio (target below 2), serum insulin, inflammatory markers, and A1C, viewing sugars strictly as the scoreboard.
- Requires patients to maintain medical supervision at intake and returns them to their physicians for any medication adjustments once sugars begin dropping naturally.
- Learned from early hiring mistakes to screen first for mission belief, then skill, and now uses paid $97 consultations to filter workshop attendees who lack genuine commitment.

Jason Shumard is a functional-medicine practitioner who scaled a virtual practice around measurable type 2 diabetes reversal through cellular repair.

episodes.title: Ep6: Glenn Broder — Workshops that train professionals to apply AI to real tasks
episodes.hook: Workshops that train professionals to apply AI to real tasks then audit every inference so the tool amplifies capability without replacing the final accountable judgment.
episodes.summary:
Glenn Broder describes a test he ran on a chat model: a story so absurd that a child would have seen through it, and after about ten exchanges the AI was telling him to move away from the windows, lock the doors, call 911 and let nobody in. He now uses that exchange when he trains people, especially children, to show that ungoverned AI is dangerous and that governed AI can do remarkable work, as long as human judgment stays in place.

His course, Human Judgment in the Age of AI, runs eight one-hour sessions: it starts with how a model actually produces an answer and why it is so confident when it is wrong, spends several sessions on governance, and ends with each student building a project of their own. With companies, his team first builds a business canon of how the business operates, works with the employees to find the bottlenecks in the workflow, and keeps the system outside the company network. Whoever signs off on the work still owns the decision.

- He calls it a cognitive jungle gym when people verify and confirm what the AI drafts, and a cognitive wheelchair when they just press send; timing the review step shows which is which.
- His test of whether someone used AI well is whether they can explain their work. If they cannot, they used it as a wheelchair.
- Students in their seventies catch the model's mistakes because they are expert in the work they are doing.
- He teaches deterministic versus probabilistic software with a wrong button that returns an error, and a model learning to fill in "the dog is chasing a ___".
- He applies the Talmudic logic he was taught as a child, questioning everything respectfully until the nuance is clear, to all of his systems, including HACS, the control layer that checks prompts going in and answers coming out against the company canon.
- His newest formulation: build your business canon outside your network, so you are never locked into one AI provider.

Glenn Broder created Human Judgment in the Age of AI to train professionals and students to keep final accountability with the human user.
